summary: An informational overview from Nortel of its Virtual Network Switching product, which presents a vendor's approach to building virtual networks. It describes the vendor's design and is not a standard.

eli5.summary: A company's explanation of how its network gear can pretend to be many separate networks at once.

questions: how does vns reduce routing hops
subtitle: A label-switching architecture for virtual networks that reduces routing hops and improves traffic management.

tldr.problem: Wide-area backbone networks face scalability, service differentiation, redundancy, and traffic containment challenges as they grow larger and carry mission-critical traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Virtual Network Switching adds a label-based switching layer that makes point-to-point links appear as a single LAN, reducing routing hops and enabling traffic segregation into logical networks with class-of-service support.
tldr.outcome: VNS was proven in production networks and provides efficient solutions for large WAN networks, but remains a vendor-specific architecture rather than an adopted standard.

today: RFC 2340 is an Informational document describing Nortel's proprietary Virtual Network Switching architecture. VNS was proven in production networks but did not become a standardized protocol. The related Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) architecture, developed by the IETF around the same time, became the industry standard for label-based switching.

sections.title: The VNS Problem
sections.content:
Wide-area networks carrying LAN traffic face five major problems: as networks grow, scalability becomes difficult with traditional topologies; service providers need to offer multiple Classes of Service instead of simple best-effort delivery; mission-critical traffic requires redundancy that is costly when implemented with additional links; network operators need simplified administration without extensive configuration; and proper traffic segregation is essential for security and performance.

Nortel's Virtual Network Switching addresses these challenges with a multi-protocol label switching architecture.
sections.eli5: Big networks have lots of problems: they get slow, they can't handle different types of traffic separately, they're hard to manage, and they can't easily keep traffic apart. VNS tries to fix all of these at once.

sections.title: How VNS Works
sections.content:
VNS is a label switching architecture that makes a network of point-to-point links appear to be a single LAN (broadcast, multiple-access media). A VNS network is organized into one or more Logical Networks (LNs), which are subsets of the physical network. Each LN has its own routing and forwarding tables, so routing decisions use only the resources available to that LN, not the entire network.

In the ISO layer model, VNS sits between the network layer (like IP) and the data link layer, presenting itself as a data link layer to higher protocols while running as a network layer above the actual media (such as ATM). Each packet receives a VNS header containing labels that tandem nodes use to forward the packet without examining the higher-layer headers.
sections.eli5: VNS puts a special label on each message that tells the network where it is going. The network just looks at the label, not at the full address, which is much faster. Each logical network is like a separate postal system inside the big network.

sections.title: The VNS Header
sections.content:
VNS defines two header formats: one for unicast (point-to-point) traffic and one for multicast (one-to-many) traffic. Both headers occupy 12 bytes of control information before the network layer header.

The unicast header contains: a Time To Live (TTL) field to prevent routing loops, a Logical Network Number (LNN) that identifies which logical network the packet belongs to, a Destination Node Identifier that uniquely identifies the egress node, a Source Node Identifier for the ingress node, a Class of Service field for traffic differentiation, a Discard Priority for congestion control, and a Load Spreading Key for traffic engineering. The multicast header adds a Multicast Group field to identify the target group within the logical network.
sections.eli5: The header is like the address on a package. It says where the package came from, where it is going, how important it is, and what type of traffic it is. The network uses this information to decide the best path.

sections.title: Routing and Forwarding
sections.content:
VNS routing is a link-state routing system similar to OSPF and PNNI. Each node maintains information about the state of locally attached links (up/down, speed, available bandwidth) and floods this information throughout the logical network when significant changes occur. All nodes maintain a complete view of the LN topology.

VNS forwarding supports both unicast and multicast modes. For unicast, the ingress node determines the best egress node and adds the VNS header; tandem nodes independently choose the next hop to that egress node using the forwarding table. For multicast, packets travel along branches of a spanning tree built from a common root node, so each node receives multicast packets only once in stable topologies.

VNS also enables traffic engineering through equal-cost multipath forwarding (spreading traffic across multiple paths of equal cost) and trunk load spreading (distributing traffic across multiple trunks between neighbors). The load spreading key, calculated at the ingress node from network-layer addresses, ensures a given flow always takes the same path and avoids packet misordering.
sections.eli5: Each node tells the others about the roads it can see. The ingress node (starting point) picks the best destination node, and all the nodes between the start and end independently figure out how to get there. For many-to-many delivery, packets travel along a tree so nothing gets duplicated.

sections.title: Logical Networks and Migration
sections.content:
Logical Networks partition a physical network into subnetworks serving different communities of interest or geographic regions. Each LN is independent: provisioning requires only a unique node ID and an LNN at configuration time, and the system automatically discovers which trunks support which LNNs at runtime. This provides significant administrative savings compared to per-link provisioning.

Multiple LNs offer several benefits: service providers can easily operate multiple private networks (Virtual Private Internets) over one physical network; protocols that broadcast or multicast heavily can be isolated to limit impact on others; network configuration can meet individual needs; and routing control traffic stays local to each LN.

VNS supports migration by running on both Frame and Cell (ATM) trunks simultaneously, allowing graceful migration from frame relay to ATM without requiring complete network overhaul. VNS can also be gradually introduced into a network, with nodes running both layer 3 routing and VNS packet switching.
sections.eli5: You can create many separate virtual networks inside one physical network. Each one is set up on a per-node basis, not per-link, which saves work. Different customer networks, different departments, or different types of traffic can each have their own logical network.
